newsitem.title: USA: Clinton close to naming pick for FCC chief, sources.
newsitem.headline: Clinton close to naming pick for FCC chief, sources.

text.p: President Clinton is close to naming William Kennard as his choice to head the Federal Communications Commission at a critical time for the regulatory agency, government and industry sources said on Thursday.

Kennard, a Democrat who is now the FCC's general counsel, is a highly regarded lawyer who would be the first black to head the five-member agency, which is overseeing the huge changes sweeping through the communications industry.
The exact timing for an announcement on the choice is not clear, although the sources said it was expected soon.

Kennard would replace Reed Hundt, who in May announced his plans to leave the agency after a stormy 3-1/2-year tenure as chairman. During that time he oversaw the implementation of last year's sweeping communications law.
The president already had nominated Kennard to become a member of the FCC before Hundt announced his departure plans.

The FCC is battling the regional Baby Bell phone companies and state phone regulators in court over landmark rules the agency adopted last August to break open the $100 billion local phone market to competition.

The departure of four of five commissioners at the agency, which also oversees the broadcast, wireless, satellite and cable TV industries, has thrown added uncertainty into the already-volatile communications business.

The president also is expected to nominate Justice Department attorney Michael Powell to fill one of two Republican seats at the FCC. Powell is the son of Colin Powell, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff who helped lead the United States and its allies to victory over Iraq in the 1991 Gulf War.

Gloria Tristani, a phone regulator from New Mexico, is expected to be named as Clinton's choice to fill a Democratic vacancy. The choice of Tristani is designed to ease the concerns of rural lawmakers worried that their interests are not adequately represented at the FCC, the sources said.
The expected Powell and Tristani nominations were not expected to be announced at the same time as the Kennard pick.

All choices require Senate confirmation. When he first announced Kennard's nomination, Clinton also nominated Harold Furchtgott-Roth, chief economist for the House Commerce Committee, to fill a Republican vacancy.
As general counsel, Kennard is credited with boosting the FCC's "win" record before federal appeals courts to 85 percent from 58 percent.

He became general counsel in December 1993. His chief rival for the FCC chairman's post was thought to be Kathleen Wallman, the former head of the FCC's Common Carrier Bureau. She is now the chief of staff for the White House's National Economic Council.
Neither of the two major political parties can control more than three of the five seats at the FCC.
